title: The Rover Trail
topic: TABLES AND GRAPHS OF TWO VARIABLES
pageTitle: Analyze Graphs of Relationships Between Two Variables
covers: how a table of values becomes ordered pairs and a graph, how to read the rate of change, and what a flat part of a graph means in the story
cert: reading and building graphs of two-variable relationships from tables and matching a graph to its story

intro.caption: Lesson 9-2 — tables and graphs of two variables. Pebble rolled out of the colony to chase a strange radio signal, and it did not come back. Its trail log is a list of numbers. To find Pebble, Esme has to turn that log into a graph and read it. Three gates and a boss stand in the way.

balloons.t: Pebble sent its trail log: hours and kilometers. If we graph it, we can read the whole trip.
Hours go first. They are the independent variable. Kilometers depend on the hours.
Bip-bip-bip! (Screen: Stopped to dig. Found a rock. Worth it.)

pages.caption: Every row of the log is an ordered pair: (hours, kilometers). The independent variable always comes first. Watch out for parts of the trail where the distance does not change.

balloons.t: Every row is a point. First number across, second number up.
Rescue rover ready! Each supply crate has a mass of 3 kilograms.
The line goes flat here. Did Pebble drive steady? Did time stop?
Boop. (Screen: Time did not stop. I stopped. Rock.)
There it is! Pebble found the signal. It's an old antenna!
A full trail map. Good work, crew. Pebble, those rocks stay outside.

win.caption: A table and a graph show the same relationship. Each row is an ordered pair (x, y) with the independent variable first. A rising line means the distance grows; a flat part means time passed while the distance stayed the same.

gates.title: Gate 1 · Read the Graph
gates.prompt:
Pebble's trail log. Hours driving is the independent variable (x). Kilometers from base is the dependent variable (y).
Hours driving (x)Km from base (y)
00
12
24
36
hints: Conceptual: an ordered pair is (x, y). The independent variable, hours, always comes first.
Procedural: for the rate of change, see how much y goes up each time x goes up by 1.

steps: Practice log: Takoda's drone flies 5 km each hour: (0, 0), (1, 5), (2, 10).
After 2 hours the drone is 10 km away, so the point is (2, 10): hours first, km second.
Each hour adds 5 km, so the rate of change is 5 km per hour.
worked.q: Which ordered pair shows "after 1 hour, 5 km"?

items.q: Which ordered pair shows "after 2 hours, Pebble is 4 km from base"?

options.fb: That puts kilometers first. The independent variable, hours, comes first: (hours, km).
The y-value is the distance. After 2 hours Pebble was 4 km away, not 2 km.
x = 0 means 0 hours, the start. At the start Pebble was at base, 0 km away.

items.label: Rate of change (km per hour):

fb.msg: 6 km is how far Pebble is after 3 hours. The rate is how far it goes in ONE hour.
3 is the number of hours. Divide the distance by the hours: km per hour.
0.5 is hours per kilometer, flipped. The rate is km for each 1 hour.

items.fbDefault: Look at the table: how many km does y go up each time x goes up by 1?

gates.pass: Two kilometers every hour, straight out. Esme marks the first part of the trail.

gates.title: Gate 2 · Build the Graph
gates.prompt:
Takoda loads the rescue rover. Each crate has a mass of 3 kg. Plot every row of the table as a point.
Crates (x)Mass in kg (y)
00
13
26
hints: Conceptual: each row of the table is one point. The number of crates is independent, so it goes across (x).
Procedural: for each row, start at the origin (0, 0), move right by the crates, then up by the kilograms.

steps: Practice table: water jugs (x) and liters (y): (1, 4) and (2, 8).
For (1, 4): start at the origin, go right 1, then up 4. Put a point.
For (2, 8): go right 2, then up 8. The points rise to the right.
worked.q: Where do you go to plot (5, 1)?

items.q: Plot all three rows of the crate table.

fb.msg: (3, 1) puts kilograms first. Crates go across (x), kilograms go up (y): (1, 3).
(6, 2) is swapped. 2 crates go across, 6 kg goes up: (2, 6).
1 crate has a mass of 3 kg, so go up 3, not 1.

items.fbDefault: Plot (0, 0), (1, 3) and (2, 6): x across first, then y up.

items.q: What label goes on the horizontal axis (x)?

options.fb: Mass depends on the crates, so it is the dependent variable. It goes on the vertical axis (y).
That is from Pebble's trail, not this table. This table pairs crates with mass.

gates.pass: Three points in a straight rising line. Takoda straps the crates down and hits the gas.

hints: Conceptual: a rising part means the distance is growing. A flat part means time passes but the distance stays the same.
Procedural: read the graph left to right, one piece at a time: up, flat, up. Tell the story of each piece.

steps: Practice graph: water in a tank goes up from day 0 to day 3, then stays flat from day 3 to day 5.
Going up: the tank is filling. Flat: the days keep passing, but the water stays the same.
Story: the pump filled the tank, then the pump was turned off.
worked.q: On a distance graph, what does a part that goes DOWN mean?
worked.a: the rover is coming back toward base

options.t: Pebble drives at one steady speed the whole time.
options.fb: A steady speed makes one straight rising line. This graph has a flat part where the distance stays at 4 km.

options.t: Pebble drives out, then drives back to base.
options.fb: Driving back would make the distance go DOWN. No part of this graph goes down.

options.t: Pebble drives out, stops to dig a rock, then drives farther.
Pebble drives out, and during the flat part no time passes.
options.fb: Time is on the horizontal axis. Along the flat part it moves from hour 2 to hour 3, so one hour passed.

items.label: Km from base at hour 3:
items.aria: Pebble's distance from base at hour 3

fb.msg: 6 would mean Pebble kept driving during the flat part. The graph stays at 4 km from hour 2 to hour 3.
3 is the hour, the x-value. Read UP to the line to find the distance.
A flat part does not mean zero. It means the distance stayed the same as before: 4 km.

items.fbDefault: Find hour 3 on the horizontal axis, then go up to the line and read the km.

gates.pass: Up, flat, up. Pebble stopped for a rock, of course. Esme follows the second stretch.

gates.title: Boss Gate · Map the Trail
gates.prompt:
Pebble's full trail to the antenna. Map it so the crew can find the way home.
Hours (x)Km from base (y)
00
12
22
34
46
hints: Conceptual: two rows with the same y-value make a flat part. The distance did not change, even though an hour passed.
Procedural: plot every row as (hours, km). For the rate, use only the rows from hour 2 to hour 4.

steps: From hour 1 to hour 2 the distance stays at 3 km. That part is flat: the rover stopped.
From hour 2 to hour 3 it goes from 3 km to 6 km: 3 km in 1 hour.
worked.q: In that practice trail, what is the rate from hour 2 to hour 3?

items.q: Plot all five rows of the trail table.

fb.msg: At hour 2 Pebble was still 2 km from base. It stopped to dig, so the distance did not change: (2, 2).
(2, 1) is swapped. Hours go across first: (1, 2).
(4, 3) is swapped. Hours go across first: (3, 4).
(6, 4) is swapped. Hours go across first: (4, 6).

items.fbDefault: Plot (0, 0), (1, 2), (2, 2), (3, 4) and (4, 6): hours across, km up.

items.q: From hour 1 to hour 2 the graph is flat. What happened?

options.fb: Going back would make the distance go down to 0. It stayed at 2 km.

options.t: Pebble stayed 2 km from base while an hour passed.
Pebble kept driving at 2 km per hour.
options.fb: If Pebble kept driving, it would be 4 km away at hour 2. Flat means the distance did not change.

options.t: The log skipped; no time passed.
options.fb: The hours go from 1 to 2, so a whole hour passed. Only the distance stayed the same.

items.label: Rate from hour 2 to hour 4 (km per hour):
items.aria: kilometers per hour from hour 2 to hour 4

fb.msg: 6 ÷ 4 uses the whole trip, including the hour Pebble was stopped. Use only hour 2 to hour 4.
6 ÷ 2 uses the distance at hour 4. But at hour 2 Pebble was already 2 km out. It went 6 − 2 = 4 km.
4 km is how far Pebble went. It took 2 hours, so divide by 2.

items.fbDefault: From hour 2 to hour 4, how many km did Pebble go, and in how many hours?

gates.pass: Trail mapped: out 2 km, a rock stop, then 2 km per hour to the antenna. The crew drives home on Pebble's tracks.

journal.heading: Lesson 9-2 — what the rover trail taught us
rows: Each row of a table is a point (x, y). The independent variable comes first: (2, 4) means 2 hours, 4 km.
The independent variable goes on the horizontal axis. The dependent variable goes on the vertical axis. They meet at the origin (0, 0).
How much y changes each time x goes up by 1. Pebble's log went up 2 km every hour.
Flat does not mean time stopped. Time kept going across; only the distance stayed the same, because Pebble stopped to dig.
journal.quote: "The graph went flat. So did I. There was a rock." — Pebble (via Idris's screen)

teacher.suggested: Use during or after lesson 9-2 (Analyze Graphs of Relationships Between Two Variables) as one focused read. Whole-class on a projector, pairs on devices, or independent practice. It covers only this lesson: turning a table of values into ordered pairs and a graph, labeling the axes, reading the rate of change, and telling the story of a graph, including what a flat part means.
standards: Use variables to represent two quantities that change in relationship to one another; write an equation for the dependent variable in terms of the independent variable; analyze the relationship using graphs and tables
